Look at the two structures and find what one has that the other has not.
Methanoic acid is H–COOH. Its carboxyl carbon carries a hydrogen, so the molecule contains
both an acid group **and** an aldehyde group, –CHO.
Ethanoic acid is CH₃–COOH, where that position is taken by a methyl group and no aldehyde
function exists.
So use a test for an aldehyde. Tollens' reagent, ammoniacal AgNO₃, is reduced by methanoic
acid and a silver mirror is deposited:
HCOOH + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 2OH⁻ ⇒ 2Ag↓ + CO₂ + 2H₂O + 4NH₃
Ethanoic acid gives no mirror.
The other three tests fail to distinguish them, because both are carboxylic acids: both turn
blue litmus red, both esterify with an alcohol, and both give CO₂ with sodium bicarbonate.
∴ Tollens' test.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|19||0|0:
In the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an alkaline electrolyte, oxygen is the species reduced,
and reduction always happens at the cathode.
At the cathode, oxygen takes up electrons and, with water, produces hydroxide:
O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ ⇒ 4OH⁻(aq)
Check it balances. Atoms: 2 O from O₂ plus 2 O from water = 4 O on the left, 4 O in 4OH⁻ ✓;
hydrogen 4 on each side ✓. Charge: −4 on the left from the electrons, −4 on the right ✓
At the anode, hydrogen is oxidised by those hydroxide ions:
2H₂ + 4OH⁻ ⇒ 4H₂O + 4e⁻
Adding the two half reactions gives option (1), 2H₂ + O₂ ⇒ 2H₂O — that is the **overall** cell
reaction, not the cathode half reaction, which is why (1) is the tempting wrong answer.
∴ O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ ⇒ 4OH⁻.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|20||0|0.s:
The Freundlich isotherm relates the amount adsorbed per gram of adsorbent to the pressure:
x/m = k·p^(1/n), with n > 1
That is a power law, so take logarithms of both sides to straighten it:
log(x/m) = log k + (1/n)·log p
Compare with y = c + mx. Plotting log(x/m) on the y axis against **log p** on the x axis gives
a straight line, of slope 1/n and intercept log k.
So the correct graph must have log p along the horizontal axis, which rules out (1) and (2) —
those plot against p itself and are curves.
Between (3) and (4), the line must cut the y axis at a positive intercept log k, not pass through
the origin, because k is not 1.
∴ graph (3).

kcet|Chemistry|2015|24||0|0.s:
Depression of freezing point is ΔTf = i·Kf·m, so the **highest** freezing point goes with the
smallest number of particles — the smallest product i × concentration.
Work out i × C for each:
(1) 0.1 M sucrose — does not dissociate, i = 1 ⇒ 0.1 × 1 = 0.1
(2) 0.01 M NaCl — gives Na⁺ + Cl⁻, i = 2 ⇒ 0.01 × 2 = 0.02 ← smallest
(3) 0.1 M NaCl — i = 2 ⇒ 0.1 × 2 = 0.2
(4) 0.01 M Na₂SO₄ — gives 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻, i = 3 ⇒ 0.01 × 3 = 0.03
The smallest is 0.02, so that solution freezes closest to 0 °C.
Note you cannot judge by concentration alone, nor by i alone — it is the product that counts.
∴ 0.01 M NaCl.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|25||0|0.s:
Two things are needed: the rate constant, and the concentration at 20 minutes.
Rate constant from the half-life:
k = 0.693 / t½ = 0.693 / 10 = 0.0693 min⁻¹
Concentration after 20 min. That is two half-lives:
12 M ⇒ 6 M at 10 min ⇒ 3 M at 20 min
Now apply the first order rate law:
rate = k[A] = 0.0693 × 3 M min⁻¹
The common slip is to use the initial 12 M and answer 0.0693 × 12; the rate is instantaneous
and must use the concentration *at that moment*.
∴ rate = 0.0693 × 3 M min⁻¹.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|26||0|0.s:
The salt must give a visible result with dilute H₂SO₄ **and** a further one with the concentrated acid.
Ba(NO₃)₂ does both.
With dilute H₂SO₄ the barium ion is precipitated at once as the sulphate, which is insoluble:
Ba(NO₃)₂ + H₂SO₄ ⇒ BaSO₄↓ (white) + 2HNO₃
With concentrated H₂SO₄ the nitrate ion reacts as well, displacing the more volatile acid and
giving the characteristic brown fumes:
2NO₃⁻ + H₂SO₄ ⇒ 2HNO₃ + SO₄²⁻, and the HNO₃ decomposes to brown NO₂
The others respond to one reagent at most: CaF₂ needs concentrated acid to give HF and does
nothing with dilute; Na₂SO₄ and Na₃PO₄ give no visible change with either.
∴ Ba(NO₃)₂.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|29||0|0:
A cyanohydrin is formed when HCN adds across the carbonyl of a ketone:
>C=O + HCN ⇒ >C(OH)–CN
Look at what attacks what. The C=O bond is polarised Cδ⁺=Oδ⁻, because oxygen is far more
electronegative, so the carbonyl carbon is electron deficient.
The attacking species is CN⁻, which has a lone pair and a negative charge — a nucleophile.
It attacks the carbonyl carbon, the π electrons shift onto oxygen to give an alkoxide, and that
alkoxide then picks up H⁺ to give the –OH.
Nothing is displaced — the π bond simply opens and both fragments of HCN are retained — so
this is an **addition**, not a substitution.
That is the hallmark of carbonyl chemistry: aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition,
while the electron-rich benzene ring undergoes electrophilic substitution.
∴ nucleophilic addition.
